There's no need for energy to reach absolute zero.

Well, it turns out temperature is a pretty normal idea that gets really complex once you start drilling down into specifics. Let me cover a few examples:

The first definition of heat that people usually give is "amount of motion in the atoms of something." That's a good place to start.

There is an 'absolute heat' for molecules because at some point, adding more energy will just break the chemical bonds and throw the whole thing into individual atoms. This energy is different from molecule to molecule, and it's called the Heat of Formation. For large polymers, a MALDI is a valuable tool because it allows us to do mass spec readings on things that normally would fly apart or polymerize into different things just from the energy of trying to ionize them!

But once you get down to atoms, you can go further. There's more in the world than just molecules, after all.

Let's imagine a piece of metal as a huge lattice of atoms, stuck together in a springy magnetic grid. If it's hot, the atoms are wiggling. If they're really hot, they may even wiggle themselves so hard that they break out of the lattice and just jumble over each other - that's a metal going from solid to liquid.

Once you get hot enough it becomes a gas, and the atoms are flying around without interacting together at all. That's as far as it goes, right? Wrong. Then there's plasma.

Turns out atoms are made up of protons and neutrons in the center, with a bunch of electrons floating around that. The electrons are attracted by static forces to the nucleus, but electrons are repelled by each other so most of the time the only way atoms interact is just between their electron clouds bumping off each other.

What happens when you're going so fast the electrons get knocked away completely? That's plasma.

Plasma is a gas of atoms with so much energy that their electrons are knocked clean off and you just have raw nuclei bouncing around. They're repelled from each other as well, so we still have mostly gas-like behavior (little balls bouncing around) but the added bonus is that now they have an overall charge and can be manipulated by magnetic/electric fields.

This is how particle accelerators work - atoms all on their own aren't very electromagnetically active (negative electrons, positive protons, they cancel each other out) so you get them so hot that the electrons get knocked off, and you can mess with the plasma without ever even touching it using fields to move it around.

Here's where things start to get weird(er) though.

Remember how we stripped off all those electrons from the nucleus? Well you can do that with heat, or you can do that with electricity. Which is which? Turns out it's all just energy. And there are a fuckton of types of energy, many of which aren't even particles. How can we talk about their temperature? Do they even have one?

Turns out even things we don't normally think of as 'things' can have a temperature. Empty space can have a temperature, black holes can have a temperature, certain kinds of light and all sorts of shit.

Because we've left the realm of particles behind, it's not helpful to talk about heat as the average motion of things. Instead we'll talk about heat as the tendency for energy to transfer. (This still makes sense - remember that in touching a hot object it transfers its energy to you)

We've got blackbody radiation, which is electromagnetic radiation given off by objects at a certain temperature. The hotter something gets, the shorter the wavelength it gives off. This is why metal glows red-hot and why the sun is yellow. It's also why infra-red cameras can tell your temperature. Turns out, the hotter a particle gets the faster it bleeds that energy off - even if there's nothing for it to bump into, it will give that energy off as radiation just into the empty space around it.

So what if we want to keep our particle hot? Well, we'd have to fill the empty space around it with a bunch of electromagnetic waves as well, so any time it gives energy off it absorbs the same amount again. Empty space can have a temperature. I don't remember the formulas exactly, but deep space is really fucking cold even by these standards. Like, a degree above absolute zero.

There is a top end to the temperature empty space can have, though. If there's too much energy in some part of space, it will turn into mass.

Yes you read that right.

E=mc2 motherfucker. Matter can turn into energy, well energy can turn into matter also. It's just a hell of a conversion rate.

If you fill space with enough energy, you'll create particles. This isn't just because of the weirdness in quantum particles also being waves - like you'll create new particles with mass as photons condense down into whatever-the-shit other things.

This is also how another poster said that black holes are the hottest thing possible - remember Hawking radiation? Black holes give off particles at the edge of their event horizon. If we use our earlier definition of temperature as "the tendency to push energy onto other things" then that event horizon has a fucking infinite tendency to push energy out and suck matter in. Interestingly enough, the theoretical hottest temperature attainable is also 0 K. Well, almost. The absolute coldest temperature is +0 K, the absolute hottest is -0 K.

If you have a closed, finite system, you can raise the temperature beyond a point where the entropy of the system actually starts decreasing because you've filled over half of all available energy levels. This is the point where your temperature goes beyond +infinity, and ends up in the negative absolute temperatures. If you heat it further and further, the temperature goes up and up, inching ever close to 0. But just as with absolute coldness, you can't reach 0 K from the negative side either.
